agree.reason: A wary reader who has quit before is likely to find a $59 trial, a 15-minute call with the dietitian and no contract an easy, low-risk step, though the page never speaks directly to their history of quitting.

honest.reason: The page drops the 'will lower your A1C' promise, reports the 10/3/1 split, admits the sample is small and medication changes weren't tracked, and makes up no figures.

works_the_facts.reason: It works out $12.90 a meal, but it leaves 37 of 88 as a raw count instead of saying 'more than 4 in 10 stay past six months' and doesn't put 10 of 14 as a share, so its most persuasive facts aren't in their strongest true form.

right_comparison.reason: The only alternative it describes is daily carb counting and label reading, and it never sets the service against the apps and earlier delivery service this reader already dropped.

qualification.reason: The A1C hedge names real limits (small group, medication not tracked) and the trial puts the cost at $59, but it gives the reader no measurable point to check, such as getting an A1C at three months.

objections.reason: Swaps, an honest note that the menu repeats every four weeks, skip-or-cancel anytime and the six-month retention figure answer the worry about quitting again, though the page never names that worry outright.

fit.reason: It is a clear sales page of about 450 words, close to the 400 asked for, with a single order button at the end.
